editorial.headline: Wholesale Paper and Cardboard: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A foreign investor cannot register wholesale paper and cardboard in Bali today: although the activity is nationally open to PMA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks it.
editorial.body:
Paper and cardboard are the paired materials at the centre of this wholesale activity. The scope is direct: it covers wholesale trade in paper and cardboard. That clarity matters. The registration describes the commercial act of supplying those materials on a wholesale basis; it does not invite a broader reading than the stated group. Paper and cardboard are named together, so the activity should keep that paired material focus. For founders, the practical starting point is therefore a business whose activity is wholesale paper and cardboard, defined by the scope itself rather than by an assumed downstream use.

At national level, the activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA and has a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Every scale named in the record sits within that national opening, from Mikro through Besar. Taken on its own national terms, that is a fully foreign-owned registration position rather than a partial foreign-stake allowance. The underlying national reference recorded here is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. None of this expands the activity’s scope: it remains wholesale trade in paper and cardboard.

Bali changes the answer decisively. This record marks the Bali status Blocked (risk class) and confirms that PMA registration is blocked. The reason is specific: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, permanently. In plain English, a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today—even though the national setting is TERBUKA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The block concerns PMA registration; it does not alter the stated definition of wholesale paper and cardboard.

This is not a national-versus-local preference that can be softened by the activity’s general openness. It is a geographical constraint on PMA registration in Bali, triggered by the stated risk classification at the Besar scale and applied island-wide under the Bali rule. A founder can accurately hold both facts at once: national policy sets a 100% foreign ceiling, while Bali blocks PMA registration for the activity. That distinction is the decision-making fact, and it should be read before treating national openness as a Bali registration outcome. For an investor, the national ceiling does not overturn the island-wide block.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness sets the ceiling, but Bali’s permanent PMA block determines the registration outcome on the island.
